edbDesc: A phenomenon that can occur in both insulating and semiconducting materials (solids, liquids, or gases), allowing very large currents to flow within materials which are otherwise good insulators. Occurs when the electric field in the material is great enough to accelerate free electrons to the point that, when they strike atoms in the material, they can knock other electrons free: the number of free electrons is thus increased rapidly as newly generated particles become part of the process.
title: Avalanche breakdown
description: In a strong enough electric field, one free electron speeds up, smashes loose another, and those two free two more, until a flood of current pours through a gas or crystal that normally blocks it. John Townsend explained the cascade in gases around 1901. It makes Geiger counters click and lets light sensors catch single photons.
effect: one fast electron knocks loose others in a cascade that suddenly lets current flow
usedIn: Avalanche photodiodes in lidar and fibre-optic receivers
strength: One electron can multiply into millions in under a microsecond, enough to turn a single particle or photon into a pulse you can count.
pickWhy: A specific effect that amplifies a single electron into a usable current. Townsend Discharge in another batch is the same cascade in a gas and should merge here.
